name: Thomas J. Stanley
tagline: A marketing professor who studied how America's quiet self-made millionaires live.
startedFrom: He was born in 1944 in the Bronx, New York. His father drove a subway car and his mother was a homemaker and secretary; the family lived in a small apartment in a blue-collar part of the Bronx. He went to college in Connecticut, worked summers at a Chevrolet dealership, did graduate work at the University of Tennessee and earned his doctorate at the University of Georgia in 1974.

evidence.claim: In 1989 he left his teaching job at Georgia State University to do independent research full time.
He wrote that he had greatly benefited 'in my own career as a small business owner'.
evidence.locator: blog post 'The Millionaire Next Door Turns 15!', 1 Nov 2011, third paragraph

evidence.claim: He quoted his own book Millionaire Women Next Door on financially independent people: 'They make their own decisions about their next destination.'
evidence.locator: blog post 'Build Wealth to Control Your Own Destiny', 13 Mar 2012, second quoted passage from Millionaire Women Next Door

evidence.claim: Reuters reported, citing his website, that in 1980 he carried out the first national survey of America's millionaires.
evidence.locator: Reuters report, 2 March 2015, paragraph after the list of his other books

evidence.claim: In 1979 he first published on the subject, after presenting a paper in New York on people he called the 'Wealthy Blue Collar Segment'.
Recalling a childhood Halloween visit to a rich neighbourhood, he wrote that twenty years later he began studying the affluent and was 'still as enthusiastic as that young trick-or-treater'.
evidence.locator: blog post 'My First Encounter with a Millionaire', 24 Aug 2009, last paragraph

evidence.claim: His daughter Sarah Stanley Fallaw writes that his work aimed at 'providing real data versus conventional wisdom about the wealthy'.
evidence.locator: post 'Thomas J. Stanley, Father & Mentor', 24 March 2015, fourth paragraph

evidence.claim: He hired his marketing student William D. Danko as a research assistant and encouraged him through his MBA and Ph.D.; in 1993 he asked Danko to be his partner on the book.
His daughter Sarah Stanley Fallaw, who worked with him on his last research projects, calls him 'my father and mentor'.
evidence.locator: post 'Thomas J. Stanley, Father & Mentor', 24 March 2015, first paragraph

evidence.claim: He wrote that The Millionaire Next Door 'was not developed in a vacuum' and that he 'had a variety of great mentors who influenced me'.
evidence.locator: blog post 'The Millionaire Next Door Turns 15!', 1 Nov 2011, first paragraph

evidence.claim: Each Christmas he and his family drove around delivering presents to the people who had done work for him that year.
evidence.locator: paragraph quoting Sarah Stanley Fallaw on Christmas

evidence.claim: On the last day of December 2001 he gave part of his speaking fees to the University of Georgia Libraries; he and his family also gave the original manuscript of The Millionaire Next Door to UGA's Hargrett Rare Book and Manuscript Library.
He wrote that he had found a strong link between giving time or money to good causes and economic success, and advised: 'give and associate with givers'.
evidence.locator: blog post 'Success Through Giving', 13 Aug 2009, last paragraph

evidence.claim: His wife Janet said that of all his successes, the one that probably brought him the most pride was his children and grandchildren.
evidence.locator: paragraph after the account of the crash

evidence.claim: The whole family often went to Georgia Bulldogs games together, and he and his wife Janet went fishing in the lakes of the North Georgia mountains.
evidence.locator: section 'An academic beginning' (football) and last section, Janet Stanley on fishing

evidence.claim: At his death he and his daughter Sarah were working together on several projects, including two new books.
evidence.locator: post 'Thomas J. Stanley, Father & Mentor', 24 March 2015, first paragraph

principles.text: Measure wealth by what you own minus what you owe, not by how much you earn or show.
principles.locator: blog post 'Wealth Is Not Income, Income Is Not Wealth', 23 Jul 2009, first paragraph

principles.text: Spend your few best hours each day on work that lasts, not on routine that eats them.
principles.locator: blog post 'To Write or To Commute?', 13 Jul 2009, first and last paragraphs

principles.text: Use hard criticism to harden your resolve instead of letting it stop you.
principles.locator: blog post 'Critics Are Needed to Build Your Resolve', 24 Feb 2015, quoted passage from The Millionaire Mind

principles.text: Give time or money to good causes, and spend time with people who give.
principles.locator: blog post 'Success Through Giving', 13 Aug 2009, last paragraph

principles.text: Build enough savings that you can say no to an employer and make your own decisions.
principles.locator: blog post 'Build Wealth to Control Your Own Destiny', 13 Mar 2012, first paragraph and quoted passages

quotes.text: Even steel cannot be hardened unless it's hammered, and it's no different with people.
quotes.locator: blog post 'Critics Are Needed to Build Your Resolve', 24 Feb 2015, quoting his book The Millionaire Mind (2000)

quotes.text: A disciplined person sets his or her sights on a lofty target, then figures out productive ways to reach the target.
quotes.locator: blog post 'Discipline: A Nutrient of Success', 14 Feb 2012, quoting his book The Millionaire Mind (2000)

quotes.text: If you want to succeed in business, give and associate with givers.
quotes.locator: blog post 'Success Through Giving', 13 Aug 2009, last sentence

definingMoment.text: In 1989 he left his teaching job at Georgia State University to research the wealthy full time. In 1993 he asked his former student William Danko to join him on a book about them. He wrote the 477-page manuscript by hand in about 180 days, about four hours a day. The Millionaire Next Door came out in 1996 with a first printing of 5,000 copies; with its sequel it spent more than 170 weeks on the New York Times best-seller list.

shadow.text: In 2001 the writer Nassim Nicholas Taleb called The Millionaire Next Door 'an extremely misleading (but almost enjoyable) book' and used it to illustrate survivorship bias: studying only the people who got rich. Stanley and his co-author William Danko had not spoken for about 15 years when Stanley died; Danko told the New York Times he did not know why. The Millionaire Next Door argued against spending much on cars, and he died in 2015 driving a 2012 Corvette; New York Times columnist Ron Lieber wrote that Stanley too had a taste for the finer things in life and asked whether that made him a hypocrite, 'or just a human being'.

councilQuestion.text: Which of your best hours this week went into work that will last, and which went to routine?

screen.notes: Real person (1944-2015), marketing professor, researcher and author, not a politician, campaigner or religious founder; no account of sexual contact with a minor or of sexual violence found; his dark side is small and documented: a critic called his research 'extremely misleading' for survivorship bias, he and his co-author had not spoken for about 15 years when he died, and he died driving a 2012 Corvette, which a New York Times columnist set against the book's advice on cars.

review.devilsAdvocate: I attacked all five draft values against the saved blog posts, the New York Times tribute, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and Reuters reports, the UGA profile, his daughter's post and Open Library search-inside of The Millionaire Mind and Fooled by Randomness. Discipline fell: both pieces of evidence were his own blog, with no witness, short of the three sources a draft-only word needs. Family from the blind pick took its place with three sources; Independence, Curiosity, Mentorship and Generosity held, Mentorship despite the unexplained 15-year silence with Danko, which stays in the shadow. All three quotes matched the book text; seven fixes tightened dates, attributions, locators and the Taleb and Lieber wording.
